texts.35:
### Contact with Europeans
[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Paul_Buffalo_and_wife_parching_wild_rice_at_their_camp_-_NARA_-_285212.tif/lossy-page1-250px-Paul_Buffalo_and_wife_parching_wild_rice_at_their_camp_-_NARA_-_285212.tif.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Paul_Buffalo_and_wife_parching_wild_rice_at_their_camp_-_NARA_-_285212.tif)
Vintage photo entitled, "Paul Buffalo and wife parching wild rice at their camp" – 1934
There is renewed interest in nutritious eating among the Ojibwe, who have been expanding community gardens in [food deserts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_deserts "Food deserts"), and have started a mobile kitchen to teach their communities about nutritious food preparation.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe#cite_note-36) The traditional Native American diet was seasonally dependent on hunting, fishing and the foraging and farming of produce and grains. The modern diet has substituted some other types of food like [frybread](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frybread "Frybread") and "Indian tacos" in place of these traditionally prepared meals. The Native Americans loss of connection to their culture is part of the "quest to reconnect to their food traditions" sparking an interest in traditional ingredients like wild rice. Other staple foods of the Ojibwe were fish, maple sugar, venison and corn. They grew beans, squash, corn and potatoes and foraged for blueberries, blackberries, choke cherries, raspberries, gooseberries and huckleberries. During the summer game animals like deer, beaver, moose, goose, duck, rabbits and bear were hunted.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe#cite_note-38)
texts.36:
### Contact with Europeans
One traditional method of making granulated sugar known among the Anishinabe was to boil [maple syrup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maple_syrup "Maple syrup") until reduced and pour into a trough, where the rapidly cooling syrup was quickly processed into maple sugar using wooden paddles.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe#cite_note-39)
texts.37:
### Contact with Europeans
#### _Manoomin_ (wild rice)
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ojibwe&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Manoomin (wild rice)")]
_Manoomin_ grown in the wild has a nutty flavor, nonuniform color, and variability in size. Ojibwe harvest wild rice in late summer and early autumn. Families gather rice grain together, called “ricing", on rice beds or _Manito Gitigaan_ (the Great Spirit's Garden). One person pushes the canoe, while the other "knocks" ripe grain into the canoe using knocking sticks. Later, once rice is processed, it is [parched](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parched_grain "Parched grain") in an iron kettle over an open fire. Once golden, it is "[jigged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jigged "Jigged")"; danced or walked on to [remove hulls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Threshing "Threshing"). Finally, the rice is [winnowed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winnowed "Winnowed"), or tossed in the air so the wind blows the lighter hull away. Wild rice is often one of the first and last foods Ojibwe people eat in their lives. Ojibwe have a reciprocal relationship with the food, taking care of it so it can thrive while using it as sustenance. Spiritual offerings including tobacco and prayers are given to ensure fruitful harvests.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMilgroomWedll202278,_80%E2%80%9381-40)

texts.6:
### Oral histories and early recorded histories
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Odawa&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Oral histories and early recorded histories")]
[![Image 2](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/An_Indian_of_ye_Outawas_Tribe_%26_his_Family_going_to_War_by_George_Townshend%2C_4th_Viscount_and_1st_Marquess_Townshend.jpg/250px-An_Indian_of_ye_Outawas_Tribe_%26_his_Family_going_to_War_by_George_Townshend%2C_4th_Viscount_and_1st_Marquess_Townshend.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:An_Indian_of_ye_Outawas_Tribe_&_his_Family_going_to_War_by_George_Townshend,_4th_Viscount_and_1st_Marquess_Townshend.jpg)
Mid-18th century sketch of an Odawa family by British soldier [George Townshend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Townshend,_1st_Marquess_Townshend "George Townshend, 1st Marquess Townshend")
According to Anishinaabeg tradition, and from recordings in [Wiigwaasabak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiigwaasabak "Wiigwaasabak") (birch bark scrolls), the Odawa people came from the eastern areas of [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America"), or [Turtle Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turtle_Island_(North_America) "Turtle Island (North America)"), and from a region called [Dawnland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawnland "Dawnland") along the East Coast (where there are numerous Algonquian-language peoples).
texts.7:
### Oral histories and early recorded histories
Directed by the _miigis_ (luminescent) beings, the [Anishinaabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anishinaabe "Anishinaabe") peoples moved inland along the [Saint Lawrence River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Lawrence_River "Saint Lawrence River"). At the "Third Stopping Place" near what is now the [Straits of Mackinac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straits_of_Mackinac "Straits of Mackinac"), Michigan, the southern group of Anishinaabeg divided into three groups, the Ojibwe, Odawa, and Potawatomi.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa_people#cite_note-hodge-10)
There is [archaeological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeological "Archaeological") evidence that the [Saugeen complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saugeen_complex "Saugeen complex") people, a [Hopewell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopewell_tradition "Hopewell tradition")-influenced group who were located on the [Bruce Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Peninsula "Bruce Peninsula") during the Middle Woodland period, may have evolved into the Odawa people. The Hopewell tradition was a widely extended trading network operating from about 200 BCE to 500 CE. Some of these peoples constructed earthwork [mounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mound_builder_(people) "Mound builder (people)") for burials, a practice that ended about 250 CE.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa_people#cite_note-ONArch-11) The Saugeen mounds have not been excavated.
texts.8:
### Oral histories and early recorded histories
The Odawa, together with the Ojibwe and Potawatomi, were part of a long-term tribal alliance called the [Council of Three Fires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Three_Fires "Council of Three Fires").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa_people#cite_note-12) Together they fought the nations of the [Haudenosaunee Confederacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haudenosaunee_Confederacy "Haudenosaunee Confederacy") (who came from the East) and the [Dakota people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dakota_people "Dakota people").
In 1615 French explorer [Samuel de Champlain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_de_Champlain "Samuel de Champlain") met 300 men of a nation which, he said, "we call _les cheueux releuez_" (modern French spelling: _cheveux relevés_ (hair lifted, raised, rolled up)), near the mouth of the [French River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_River_(Ontario) "French River (Ontario)"). Of these, he said:
> Their arms consisted only of a bow and arrows, a buckler of boiled leather and the club. They wore no breech clouts, their bodies were tattooed in many fashions and designs, their faces painted and their noses pierced.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa_people#cite_note-burton-7)
In 1616, Champlain left the Wendat villages and visited the _cheueux releuez_, who lived westward from the lands of the [Wendat Confederacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wendat_people "Wendat people").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa_people#cite_note-hodge-10)
texts.9:
### Oral histories and early recorded histories
The _[Jesuit Relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesuit\_Relations "Jesuit Relations")_ of 1667 reported that three tribes lived in the same town: the Odawa, the Kiskakon Odawa, and the Sinago Odawa. All three tribes spoke the same language.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa_people#cite_note-13)
Due to the extensive trade network maintained by the Odawa, many of the North American interior nations became known to Europeans by the names the Odawa used for them (exonyms), rather than by the nations' own names (endonyms). For example, these exonyms include _Winnebago_ (from _Wiinibiigoo_) for the [Ho-Chunk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ho-Chunk "Ho-Chunk"), and [Sioux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sioux "Sioux") (from _Naadawensiw_) for the Dakota. From the early days of the colony of [New France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_France "New France"), the Odawa became so important to the French and Canadians in [fur trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fur_trade "Fur trade") that before 1670, colonists in [Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec "Quebec") (then called [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_(New_France) "Canada (New France)")) usually referred to any Algonquian speaker from the Great Lakes region as an Odawa. In their own language, the Odawa (like the Ojibwe) identified as Anishinaabe (_Neshnabek_) meaning "people".
texts.10:
### Oral histories and early recorded histories
The mostly highly prized fur was beaver, popular in Europe. Other furs traded included deer, marten, raccoon, fox, otter, and muskrat. In exchange the Odawa received "hatchets, knives, kettles, traps, needles, fish hooks, cloth and blankets, jewelry and decorative items, and later firearms and alcohol".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa_people#cite_note-14) Up to the time of [Nicolas Perrot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Perrot "Nicolas Perrot"), the Odawa had a monopoly on all fur trade that came through [Green Bay, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Bay,_Wisconsin "Green Bay, Wisconsin"), or [Sault Ste. Marie, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sault_Ste._Marie,_Michigan "Sault Ste. Marie, Michigan"). They allegedly did "their best to exploit" the tribes in those areas "who did not use the canoe, by bartering with them bits of iron and steel and worn-out European articles for extravagant quantities of furs". For example, "the Crees gave the Ottawas 'all their beaver robes for old knives, blunted awls, wretched nets and kettles used until they were past service.'"[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa_people#cite_note-15)
[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4b/Chief_Pontiac_%281%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chief_Pontiac_(1).jpg)
Odawa warrior with [gunstock war club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstock_war_club "Gunstock war club")
texts.11:
### Oral histories and early recorded histories
The Odawa had disputes and warfare with other tribes, particularly over the lucrative fur trade. For example, the tribe once waged war against the [Mascouten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mascouten "Mascouten"). In the mid-17th century the Odawa allied with other Algonquian tribes around the Great Lakes against the powerful [Mohawk people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohawk_people "Mohawk people") (of present-day New York) and their Haudenosaunee allies in the [Beaver Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaver_Wars "Beaver Wars"). The European introduction of guns and other weapons to some of their trading partners had disrupted the traditional balance of power in the region and changed economic risks and rewards. All indigenous peoples on both sides were disrupted or decimated; some groups, such as the Iroquoian-speaking [Erie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erie_people "Erie people"), were exterminated as tribes. But by the mid-17th century, the tribes were more severely affected by new infectious diseases than warfare. Lacking acquired [immunity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immunity_(medical) "Immunity (medical)") to these European diseases, they suffered epidemics with high fatalities.
In 1701, the French colonists built [Fort Detroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Detroit "Fort Detroit") and established a trading post. Many Odawa moved there from their traditional homeland of Manitoulin Island near the Bruce Peninsula,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa_people#cite_note-hodge-10) and [Wyandot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyandot_people "Wyandot people") also moved near the post. Some Odawa had already settled across northern Michigan in the Lower Peninsula, and more bands established villages around and south of Detroit. Their area extended into present-day Ohio.
texts.12:
### Oral histories and early recorded histories
With movements of the tribes in relation to warfare and colonial encroachment, the tribes settled in roughly the following pattern: "Sandwiched between the French, in the north and west, and the English, in the south and east, the [Miami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_people "Miami people") settled in present-day Indiana and western Ohio; the Ottawa settled in Northwest Ohio along the Maumee, the Auglaize, and the Blanchard rivers; the [Wyandot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyandot_people "Wyandot people") settled in Central Ohio; the [Shawnee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shawnee "Shawnee") in Southwest Ohio; and the [Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware "Delaware") (Lenape) in Southeast and Eastern Ohio."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa_people#cite_note-tanner-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa_people#cite_note-17)
texts.13:
### Oral histories and early recorded histories
In the mid-18th century, the Odawa allied with their [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") trading partners against the [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") in the [Seven Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Years'_War "Seven Years' War"), known as the [French and Indian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_and_Indian_War "French and Indian War") in the North American colonies. They made raids against Anglo-American colonists. The Odawa chief [Pontiac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontiac_(Ottawa_leader) "Pontiac (Ottawa leader)")[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa_people#cite_note-auto-18) has historically been reported to have been born at the confluence of the Maumee and Auglaize rivers, where modern [Defiance, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defiance,_Ohio "Defiance, Ohio"), later developed. In 1763, after the British had defeated France, Pontiac led a [rebellion against the British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontiac's_War "Pontiac's War"), but he was unable to prevent British colonial settlement of the region.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa_people#cite_note-19)
texts.14:
### Oral histories and early recorded histories
A decade later, Chief [Egushawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egushawa "Egushawa") (also spelled Agushawa), who had a village at the mouth of the [Maumee River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maumee_River "Maumee River") on [Lake Erie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Erie "Lake Erie") (where Toledo later developed), led the Odawa as an ally of the British in the [American Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War"). He hoped to build on their support to exclude European-American colonists from his territory in northwest Ohio and southern Michigan.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa_people#cite_note-autogenerated203-20) The defeat of the British by the United States had a far-ranging influence on British-allied Native American tribes, as many were forced to cede their land to the United States.
Following the Revolutionary War, in the 1790s, Egushawa, together with numerous members of other regional tribes, including the Wyandot and Council of Three Fires, Shawnee, Lenape, and Mingo, fought the United States in a series of battles and campaigns in what became known as the [Northwest Indian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Indian_War "Northwest Indian War"). The Indians hoped to repulse the European-American pioneers coming to settle west of the Appalachian Mountains, but were finally defeated.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa_people#cite_note-autogenerated203-20)
texts.15:
### Oral histories and early recorded histories
In 1792 President George Washington sent Major Alexander Truman, his servant William Lynch, and guide/interpreter William Smalley on a peace mission to the tribes. Truman and Lynch were killed; Truman was apparently killed prior to April 20, 1792, at Lower Tawa Town, an Ottawa village (Ottawa, Putnam County Ohio). In a campaign during 1794, [Anthony Wayne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Wayne "Anthony Wayne") built a string of forts in the upper Maumee River watershed, including [Fort Defiance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Defiance_(Ohio) "Fort Defiance (Ohio)"), across the river from the site of Pontiac's birth. While the British had encouraged the Native American efforts, they did not want to get drawn into open conflict again with the United States and withdrew from offering direct support to the tribes. Wayne's army defeated several hundred members of the Indian confederacy at the [Battle of Fallen Timbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Fallen_Timbers "Battle of Fallen Timbers"), near the future site of [Maumee, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maumee,_Ohio "Maumee, Ohio") and about 11 miles upriver of present-day [Toledo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toledo,_Ohio "Toledo, Ohio").
texts.16:
### Oral histories and early recorded histories
#### Raid on Pickawillany
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Odawa&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Raid on Pickawillany")]
In the winter of 1751–1752, [Charles Langlade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Michel_de_Langlade "Charles Michel de Langlade") began assembling an allied war party of Odawa, Potawatomi, and Ojibwe warriors who traveled to [Pickawillany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pickawillany "Pickawillany"). They attacked the village in mid-morning on June 21, 1752, and killed thirteen Miami men and captured five English traders. Down to as few as twenty warriors the Miami tried to negotiate terms of surrender, and Langlade promised to allow the Miami men to return home if they handed over the English. The Miami sent only three of the five Englishmen. When the Englishmen reached Langlade's lines, one of his men stabbed one of them to death, scalped the Englishman, and ripped his heart out and ate it in front of the Miami men. Langlade's men seized the Miami chief [Memeskia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memeskia "Memeskia"). He was killed, boiled and eaten in front of his warriors. Afterward the Odawa released the Miami women and left for Detroit with four captured Englishmen and more than $300,000 worth (in today's dollars[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_]) of trade goods.
This French-led victory over the English is believed to have led to the French and Indian War and contributed to the Seven Years' War on the European continent.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa_people#cite_note-21)
texts.17:
### Treaties and removals
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Odawa&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Treaties and removals")]
In 1795, under the [Treaty of Greenville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Greenville "Treaty of Greenville"), the Odawa and other members of the Western Confederacy ceded all of Ohio to the United States, except the northwest area. This was part of the area controlled by the Detroit Odawa.
In 1807, the Detroit Odawa joined three other tribes, the Ojibwe, Potawatomi and [Wyandot people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyandot_people "Wyandot people"), in signing the [Treaty of Detroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Detroit "Treaty of Detroit") under pressure from the United States. The agreement, between the tribes and [William Hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hull "William Hull"), representing the [Michigan Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Territory "Michigan Territory"), gave the United States a large portion of today's [Southeastern Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Michigan "Southeastern Michigan") and a section of northwest [Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio "Ohio") near the Maumee River.
Many Odawa bands moved away from the European Americans into northern Michigan. The tribes retained communal control of relatively small pockets of land in the territory of the Maumee River.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa_people#cite_note-WDL-22) Bands of Odawa-occupied areas are known as Roche de Boeuf[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa_people#cite_note-23) and Wolf Rapids on the upper Maumee River.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa_people#cite_note-sultzman-24)
texts.18:
### Treaties and removals
In 1817, in the first treaty involving land cessions after the War of 1812, the Ohio Odawa ceded their lands, accepting [reservations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_historical_Indian_reservations_in_the_United_States "List of historical Indian reservations in the United States") at [Blanchard's Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanchard's_Fork_Reserve,_Ohio "Blanchard's Fork Reserve, Ohio") and the [Little Auglaize River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Auglaize_River "Little Auglaize River") in Ohio (a total of 34 square miles or 88 square kilometres). These were only reserves, for which they were paid annuities for ten years. Pressure continued to build against the Odawa as European-American settlers moved into the area.
After passage of the [Indian Removal Act of 1830](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Removal_Act_of_1830 "Indian Removal Act of 1830"), the US government arranged for the Odawa to cede their reserves in 1831. The four following bands eventually all removed to areas of Kansas, then part of [Indian Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Territory "Indian Territory"): the Blanchard's Creek, Little Auglaize, Roche de Boeuf, and Wolf Rapids bands.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa_people#cite_note-sultzman-24)
texts.19:
### Treaties and removals
The population of the different Odawa groups has been estimated. In 1906, the Ojibwe and Odawa on [Manitoulin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manitoulin_Island "Manitoulin Island") and [Cockburn Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cockburn_Island_(Ontario) "Cockburn Island (Ontario)") were 1,497, of whom about half were Odawa. There were 197 Odawa listed as associated with the Seneca School in Oklahoma, where some Odawa had settled after the American Civil War. In 1900 in Michigan there were 5,587 scattered Ojibwe and Odawa, of whom about two-thirds are Odawa.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa_people#cite_note-hodge-10)
In the early 21st century, the total number of enrolled members of the federally recognized [Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa_Tribe_of_Oklahoma "Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma") numbers about 4,700. There are about 10,000 persons who identify as Odawa in the United States, with the majority in Michigan. Another several thousand live in Ontario, Canada.
texts.20:
### Treaties and removals
There has been one major anthropological study of the [Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Traverse_Band_of_Ottawa_and_Chippewa_Indians "Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians"). [Jane Willetts Ettawageshik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Willets_Ettawageshik "Jane Willets Ettawageshik") devoted approximately two years of study in the Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians community. [Ettawageshik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Willets_Ettawageshik "Jane Willets Ettawageshik") recorded [Anishinaabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anishinaabe "Anishinaabe") stories that speak of how the Anishinaabe people related to their land, to their people, and various other means of communicating their values, outlooks and histories in and around Northern Michigan. These stories have been translated into English by Howard Webkamigada and published as the book _Ottawa Stories from the Springs_.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa_people#cite_note-25)
The following are or were Odawa villages:

# Hannibal Hamlin
Colored postcard of the Hamlin homestead. Photo: Collections of Hamlin Memorial Library and Museum.
Hannibal Hamlin was an attorney, politician, and American vice president to Abraham Lincoln. Born in the Town of Paris when Maine was still a district of Massachusetts, Hamlin was a descendent of Plymouth colonists. He studied law under Samuel Fessenden, and after being admitted to the bar, opened his own firm in Hampden.
Hamlin served in a number of political offices over the course of his career, first in the Maine House of Representatives where he helped negotiate the end of hostilities during the Aroostook War. Later, he served in the US House of Representatives and Senate as a Democrat, but his staunch abolitionist sentiments pushed him from the Democratic Party to the Republican Party in 1856.
In 1857, Hamlin served Maine as governor, but after about six weeks, he resigned to return to the Senate. In 1860, he was nominated as the Republican party's pick for vice president on the ticket with Abraham Lincoln. They won the election and worked well together, with Hamlin supporting the Emancipation Proclamation.
After his term as vice president, Hamlin continued serving as a senator until 1881, then as ambassador to Spain from 1881 to 1882, and subsequently retired from public service to Bangor. Hamlin purchased the Italianate house that now bears his name in 1851, and he lived there until his death in 1891. The house, located on 5th Street, was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1979.
Hamlin is remembered today as Maine's only vice president and for his support of abolitionist causes. Towns and parks throughout the country are named in Hamlin's honor, and Maine honors his memory through Hamlin Peak in Piscataquis County, a building at University of Maine at Orono, the Hannibal Hamlin Memorial Library in Paris, as well as a bronze statue in downtown Bangor.

# U.S. Vice Presidents: Hannibal Hamlin
## Biography
Hannibal Hamlin, (born Aug. 27, 1809, Paris Hill,Maine, U.S.—died July 4, 1891,Bangor, Maine), 15th vice president of the United States(1861–65) in the Republican administration of President Abraham Lincoln. Hamlin was elected to the United States House of Representatives in 1842 and to the Senate in 1848. In his first term as a senator, he took an antislavery position on sectional issues and left the Democratic Party in 1856 because of its endorsement of the Kansas-Nebraska Act(1854), which proponents of abolitionism had attacked as a capitulation to the interests of the slave states.He was elected Maine’s first Republican governor (1856) but resigned in February 1857 to return to the Senate.

# U.S. Vice Presidents: Henry Wilson
## Did You Know?
Vice President Wilson...
*   ...born Jeremiah Jones Colbath because his father named him after a wealthy neighbor who was a childless bachelor, hoping that this gesture might result in an inheritance. The reasons given for him changing his name vary.  
*   ...enriched his paltry education by borrowing books from his neighbors. He studied History and biographies.  
*   ...started a new political anti-slavery party called Free Soil Party.

# U.S. Vice Presidents: Henry Wilson
## Biography
Henry Wilson(born Jeremiah Jones Colbath; February 16, 1812 – November 22, 1875) was the 18th vice president of the United States(1873–75) and a senator from Massachusetts(1855–73). Before and during the American Civil War, he was a leading Republican, and a strong opponent of slavery. Wilson devoted his energies to the destruction of the "Slave Power" – the faction of slave owners and their political allies which anti-slavery Americans saw as dominating the country.Henry Wilson was born in Farmington, New Hampshire, on February 16, 1812, one of several children born to Winthrop and Abigail (Witham) Colbath.His father named him Jeremiah Jones Colbath after a wealthy neighbor who was a childless bachelor, vainly hoping that this gesture might result in an inheritance.Winthrop Colbath was a militia veteran of the War of 1812 who worked as a day laborer and hired himself out to local farms and businesses, in addition to occasionally running a sawmill.

# U.S. Vice Presidents: Hannibal Hamlin
## Did You Know?
Vice President Hamlin...
*   ...maintained his stance against slavery and his work for the integration of former slaves into society.  
*   ...advised President Abraham Lincoln on the Emancipation Proclamation demanding the end of slavery in the South.  
*   ...was appointed by President James Garfield as a diplomat to Spain.

# U.S. Vice Presidents: Hannibal Hamlin
## Biography
Hannibal Hamlin, (born Aug. 27, 1809, Paris Hill,Maine, U.S.—died July 4, 1891,Bangor, Maine), 15th vice president of the United States(1861–65) in the Republican administration of President Abraham Lincoln. Hamlin was elected to the United States House of Representatives in 1842 and to the Senate in 1848. In his first term as a senator, he took an antislavery position on sectional issues and left the Democratic Party in 1856 because of its endorsement of the Kansas-Nebraska Act(1854), which proponents of abolitionism had attacked as a capitulation to the interests of the slave states.He was elected Maine’s first Republican governor (1856) but resigned in February 1857 to return to the Senate.

# Hannibal Hamlin
Colored postcard of the Hamlin homestead. Photo: Collections of Hamlin Memorial Library and Museum.
Hannibal Hamlin was an attorney, politician, and American vice president to Abraham Lincoln. Born in the Town of Paris when Maine was still a district of Massachusetts, Hamlin was a descendent of Plymouth colonists. He studied law under Samuel Fessenden, and after being admitted to the bar, opened his own firm in Hampden.
Hamlin served in a number of political offices over the course of his career, first in the Maine House of Representatives where he helped negotiate the end of hostilities during the Aroostook War. Later, he served in the US House of Representatives and Senate as a Democrat, but his staunch abolitionist sentiments pushed him from the Democratic Party to the Republican Party in 1856.
In 1857, Hamlin served Maine as governor, but after about six weeks, he resigned to return to the Senate. In 1860, he was nominated as the Republican party's pick for vice president on the ticket with Abraham Lincoln. They won the election and worked well together, with Hamlin supporting the Emancipation Proclamation.
After his term as vice president, Hamlin continued serving as a senator until 1881, then as ambassador to Spain from 1881 to 1882, and subsequently retired from public service to Bangor. Hamlin purchased the Italianate house that now bears his name in 1851, and he lived there until his death in 1891. The house, located on 5th Street, was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1979.
Hamlin is remembered today as Maine's only vice president and for his support of abolitionist causes. Towns and parks throughout the country are named in Hamlin's honor, and Maine honors his memory through Hamlin Peak in Piscataquis County, a building at University of Maine at Orono, the Hannibal Hamlin Memorial Library in Paris, as well as a bronze statue in downtown Bangor.

# U.S. Vice Presidents: Henry Wilson
## Did You Know?
Vice President Wilson...
*   ...born Jeremiah Jones Colbath because his father named him after a wealthy neighbor who was a childless bachelor, hoping that this gesture might result in an inheritance. The reasons given for him changing his name vary.  
*   ...enriched his paltry education by borrowing books from his neighbors. He studied History and biographies.  
*   ...started a new political anti-slavery party called Free Soil Party.

# U.S. Vice Presidents: Henry Wilson
## Biography
Henry Wilson(born Jeremiah Jones Colbath; February 16, 1812 – November 22, 1875) was the 18th vice president of the United States(1873–75) and a senator from Massachusetts(1855–73). Before and during the American Civil War, he was a leading Republican, and a strong opponent of slavery. Wilson devoted his energies to the destruction of the "Slave Power" – the faction of slave owners and their political allies which anti-slavery Americans saw as dominating the country.Henry Wilson was born in Farmington, New Hampshire, on February 16, 1812, one of several children born to Winthrop and Abigail (Witham) Colbath.His father named him Jeremiah Jones Colbath after a wealthy neighbor who was a childless bachelor, vainly hoping that this gesture might result in an inheritance.Winthrop Colbath was a militia veteran of the War of 1812 who worked as a day laborer and hired himself out to local farms and businesses, in addition to occasionally running a sawmill.

—Henry Wilson
> “The natural equality of all men I believe in, as far as rights are concerned.”
—Henry Wilson
> “Equality before the law of all men, no matter where they born, or from what race they sprung, is the sentiment of the people.”
—Henry Wilson
> “The idea which pervades our Constitution; that all men of every race are equal before the laws.”
—Henry Wilson

# List of longest streams of Minnesota
Out of the 6,564 streams that flow through the [U.S. State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._State "U.S. State") of [Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota "Minnesota"), there are 114 streams that are at least 30 miles long. The second longest river in the United States, the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River"), originates in Minnesota before flowing south to the [Gulf of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico"). The longest river entirely within the state of Minnesota is the [Minnesota River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_River "Minnesota River"). Other rivers over 200 miles long include the [Red River of the North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_River_of_the_North "Red River of the North"), [Des Moines River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Des_Moines_River "Des Moines River"), [Cedar River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_River_(Iowa_River_tributary) "Cedar River (Iowa River tributary)"), [Wapsipinicon River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wapsipinicon_River "Wapsipinicon River"), [Little Sioux River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Sioux_River "Little Sioux River"), and [Roseau River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roseau_River_(Manitoba%E2%80%93Minnesota) "Roseau River (Manitoba–Minnesota)").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_longest_streams_of_Minnesota#cite_note-MNDNR-2)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_longest_streams_of_Minnesota#cite_note-Longest-3)

# List of longest streams of Minnesota
Sections of several of the longest rivers define sections of the Minnesota border.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_longest_streams_of_Minnesota#cite_note-4) The Red River of the North forms the border with [North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dakota "North Dakota") to the west. The [Bois de Sioux River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bois_de_Sioux_River "Bois de Sioux River") forms the border with [South Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Dakota "South Dakota") to the west. The Mississippi River, [St. Croix River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Croix_River_(Wisconsin-Minnesota) "St. Croix River (Wisconsin-Minnesota)"), and the [St. Louis River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Louis_River_(Lake_Superior_tributary) "Saint Louis River (Lake Superior tributary)") form the border with [Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin "Wisconsin") to the east. The [Rainy River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainy_River_(Minnesota%E2%80%93Ontario) "Rainy River (Minnesota–Ontario)") and [Pigeon River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pigeon_River_(Minnesota-Ontario) "Pigeon River (Minnesota-Ontario)") form the border with [Ontario, Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario,_Canada "Ontario, Canada") to the north.
Minnesota contains three major [drainage basins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drainage_basin "Drainage basin") with waters from Minnesota rivers flowing south, north, or east.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_longest_streams_of_Minnesota#cite_note-MNDNR-2) These major drainage basins meet in a [triple divide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_divide "Triple divide") point called the Hill of Three Waters, just north of [Hibbing, Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hibbing,_Minnesota "Hibbing, Minnesota").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_longest_streams_of_Minnesota#cite_note-5)

# List of longest streams of Minnesota
*   The Mississippi River drains south to the **[Gulf of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico").** In Minnesota, this basin is traditionally subdivided into the following major sub-basins:   
    *   [Headwaters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Headwaters_water_resource_subregion "Mississippi Headwaters water resource subregion") of the Mississippi River (above [St. Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Paul,_Minnesota "Saint Paul, Minnesota"))  
    *   [Minnesota River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_River "Minnesota River") drainage basin (17,000 sq mi (44,000 km 2))  
    *   [St. Croix River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Croix_River_(Wisconsin%E2%80%93Minnesota) "St. Croix River (Wisconsin–Minnesota)") drainage basin (7,700 sq mi (20,000 km 2))  
    *   Lower portion of the [Upper Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Mississippi_River "Upper Mississippi River") (Below St. Paul). Some of these rivers discharge into the Mississippi within the borders of Minnesota, and some farther south, including the [Des Moines River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Des_Moines_River "Des Moines River"), the [Cedar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_River_(Iowa_River_tributary) "Cedar River (Iowa River tributary)") / [Iowa River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa_River "Iowa River"), and others  
    *   Tributaries of the [Missouri River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_River "Missouri River") also have drainage basins in far southwest Minnesota

# List of longest streams of Minnesota
*   Water flows to the north in the [**Hudson Bay/Arctic**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Bay_drainage_basin "Hudson Bay drainage basin") drainage basin (3,861,400 sq mi (10,001,000 km 2)), which includes the [Red River of the North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_River_of_the_North "Red River of the North") drainage basin (111,004 sq mi (287,500 km 2)) and [Lake of the Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_of_the_Woods "Lake of the Woods") drainage basin (13,805 sq mi (35,750 km 2))—of which 7,285 sq mi (18,870 km 2) is in Minnesota.  
*   The **[Great Lakes Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes_Basin "Great Lakes Basin")** to the east includes the [Lake Superior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Superior "Lake Superior") drainage basin in Minnesota and Wisconsin (49,300 sq mi (128,000 km 2)).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_longest_streams_of_Minnesota#cite_note-6) Minnesota water flows eastward through the Great Lakes to the [Atlantic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean").

# List of longest streams of Minnesota
Out of the 6,564 streams that flow through the [U.S. State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._State "U.S. State") of [Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota "Minnesota"), there are 114 streams that are at least 30 miles long. The second longest river in the United States, the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River"), originates in Minnesota before flowing south to the [Gulf of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico"). The longest river entirely within the state of Minnesota is the [Minnesota River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_River "Minnesota River"). Other rivers over 200 miles long include the [Red River of the North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_River_of_the_North "Red River of the North"), [Des Moines River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Des_Moines_River "Des Moines River"), [Cedar River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_River_(Iowa_River_tributary) "Cedar River (Iowa River tributary)"), [Wapsipinicon River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wapsipinicon_River "Wapsipinicon River"), [Little Sioux River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Sioux_River "Little Sioux River"), and [Roseau River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roseau_River_(Manitoba%E2%80%93Minnesota) "Roseau River (Manitoba–Minnesota)").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_longest_streams_of_Minnesota#cite_note-MNDNR-2)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_longest_streams_of_Minnesota#cite_note-Longest-3)

# List of longest streams of Minnesota
Sections of several of the longest rivers define sections of the Minnesota border.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_longest_streams_of_Minnesota#cite_note-4) The Red River of the North forms the border with [North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dakota "North Dakota") to the west. The [Bois de Sioux River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bois_de_Sioux_River "Bois de Sioux River") forms the border with [South Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Dakota "South Dakota") to the west. The Mississippi River, [St. Croix River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Croix_River_(Wisconsin-Minnesota) "St. Croix River (Wisconsin-Minnesota)"), and the [St. Louis River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Louis_River_(Lake_Superior_tributary) "Saint Louis River (Lake Superior tributary)") form the border with [Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin "Wisconsin") to the east. The [Rainy River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainy_River_(Minnesota%E2%80%93Ontario) "Rainy River (Minnesota–Ontario)") and [Pigeon River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pigeon_River_(Minnesota-Ontario) "Pigeon River (Minnesota-Ontario)") form the border with [Ontario, Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario,_Canada "Ontario, Canada") to the north.
Minnesota contains three major [drainage basins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drainage_basin "Drainage basin") with waters from Minnesota rivers flowing south, north, or east.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_longest_streams_of_Minnesota#cite_note-MNDNR-2) These major drainage basins meet in a [triple divide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_divide "Triple divide") point called the Hill of Three Waters, just north of [Hibbing, Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hibbing,_Minnesota "Hibbing, Minnesota").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_longest_streams_of_Minnesota#cite_note-5)

# List of longest streams of Minnesota
*   The Mississippi River drains south to the **[Gulf of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico").** In Minnesota, this basin is traditionally subdivided into the following major sub-basins:   
    *   [Headwaters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Headwaters_water_resource_subregion "Mississippi Headwaters water resource subregion") of the Mississippi River (above [St. Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Paul,_Minnesota "Saint Paul, Minnesota"))  
    *   [Minnesota River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_River "Minnesota River") drainage basin (17,000 sq mi (44,000 km 2))  
    *   [St. Croix River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Croix_River_(Wisconsin%E2%80%93Minnesota) "St. Croix River (Wisconsin–Minnesota)") drainage basin (7,700 sq mi (20,000 km 2))  
    *   Lower portion of the [Upper Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Mississippi_River "Upper Mississippi River") (Below St. Paul). Some of these rivers discharge into the Mississippi within the borders of Minnesota, and some farther south, including the [Des Moines River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Des_Moines_River "Des Moines River"), the [Cedar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_River_(Iowa_River_tributary) "Cedar River (Iowa River tributary)") / [Iowa River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa_River "Iowa River"), and others  
    *   Tributaries of the [Missouri River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_River "Missouri River") also have drainage basins in far southwest Minnesota
texts.9:
# List of longest streams of Minnesota
*   Water flows to the north in the [**Hudson Bay/Arctic**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Bay_drainage_basin "Hudson Bay drainage basin") drainage basin (3,861,400 sq mi (10,001,000 km 2)), which includes the [Red River of the North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_River_of_the_North "Red River of the North") drainage basin (111,004 sq mi (287,500 km 2)) and [Lake of the Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_of_the_Woods "Lake of the Woods") drainage basin (13,805 sq mi (35,750 km 2))—of which 7,285 sq mi (18,870 km 2) is in Minnesota.  
*   The **[Great Lakes Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes_Basin "Great Lakes Basin")** to the east includes the [Lake Superior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Superior "Lake Superior") drainage basin in Minnesota and Wisconsin (49,300 sq mi (128,000 km 2)).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_longest_streams_of_Minnesota#cite_note-6) Minnesota water flows eastward through the Great Lakes to the [Atlantic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean").

# List of longest streams of Minnesota
## Table of longest streams
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_longest_streams_of_Minnesota&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Table of longest streams")]
A sortable table below lists the 114 streams flowing in Minnesota that have a total length greater than or equal to 30 miles. The stream's tributary and watershed are given. The source or mouth of some streams is in other U.S. states or Canadian provinces. Other than border rivers, the only rivers that originate in other states are the Little Minnesota River (South Dakota), St. Croix River (Wisconsin), and Upper Tamarack River (Wisconsin). The 21 streams that are not entirely within the state are indicated by a † after the order number. The coordinates and location county of the mouth and source of the stream are indicated, as well as the [United States Geological Survey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Geological_Survey "United States Geological Survey") (USGS) [Geographic Names Information System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geographic_Names_Information_System "Geographic Names Information System") ID and other references and notes.[[note 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_longest_streams_of_Minnesota#cite_note-7) Lengths and elevations are derived from the National Elevation Dataset or reference to it in the USGS GNIS Database.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_longest_streams_of_Minnesota#cite_note-8) A link to an Open Street Map template is listed at the top of this article that will generate a map showing the source and mouth coordinates of all of these streams. For consistency and accuracy, the sources for this information are primarily data from the USGS [GeoNames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GeoNames "GeoNames") and National Elevation database, supplemented by other sources.

## Rivers and Waterways in Iowa
Iowa’s river systems flow across gently rolling plains and fertile farmland, with most waterways draining into the Mississippi and Missouri rivers. The state is bordered by these two major rivers, while interior rivers like the Des Moines and Cedar play an important role in agriculture and local water supply. Northern and central regions feature smaller tributaries, while southern areas have wider river valleys. Iowa also includes several reservoirs and natural lakes that support recreation, flood control, and water management.

Source: https://www.foriowa.org/iowa-stories/iowa-story.php?namer=true&isid=3
Title: Old Gold: What's in a Name?
Chunks: 0,1,2
For the University of Iowa, lots of history and a little confusion
![Image 1: The Pentacrest](https://www.foriowa.org/iowa-stories/images/0418OldGold3.png)Frederick W. Kent Collection of Photographs, UI Special Collections The University of Iowa’s Pentacrest in 1958.
**_Editor’s note: In Old Gold, University archivist David McCartney looks back at the UI’s history and tradition through materials housed in University Archives, Department of Special Collections, University of Iowa Libraries._**
If Old Gold had a list of top-10-asked reference questions at the University Archives (and well he should), surely one of them would be: When did the State University of Iowa become known simply as the University of Iowa?
Variations on that theme include: Weren’t we once also known as Iowa State University? Aren’t we still officially the State University of Iowa? Has confusion ensued?
The short answers are Oct. 22, 1964; sort of; yes; and yes. It’s also correct to say that our esteemed institution has always been named the State University of Iowa. It’s complicated, as they say.
[![Image 2: Title Page](https://www.foriowa.org/iowa-stories/images/0418OldGold2.png)](https://www.foriowa.org/iowa-stories/iowa-story.php?namer=true&isid=3#)General Catalogs Collection (RG 01.08)Title page from the 1870 general catalog.
Some background: The State University of Iowa was established in 1847 as the second official act of the General Assembly of Iowa. Lawmakers declared that the fledgling school would serve as the state’s institution of higher learning, one that would provide the state its future doctors, lawyers, and other professionals.The state university, if you will. Eleven years later, in 1858, legislators established the Iowa Agricultural College and Model Farm at Ames. And in 1876, the Iowa State Normal School in Cedar Falls, a teacher-training academy, was founded.

During these early years of public higher education in Iowa, only the Iowa City institution included the word university in its title. This exclusive status seemed to allow SUI administrators to take liberties with the school’s name, referring informally to it in catalogs and other publications as “Iowa State University” during a good part of the late 1800s. The practice, which never officially changed the SUI name, appeared to have ended by the 1890s. Official Board of Regents, State of Iowa, meeting minutes throughout this time consistently referred to “State University of Iowa,” however.
In 1898, meanwhile, the Ames campus was renamed Iowa State College of Agricultural and Mechanic Arts; in 1959 it was again changed to its present-day Iowa State University of Science and Technology. The Cedar Falls campus changed its name in 1909 to Iowa State Teachers College, and again in 1961 to the State College of Iowa before finally adopting the University of Northern Iowa in 1967.
Let’s see: By the early 1960s, Iowa’s three public institutions shared the words state and Iowa. What’s worse, two of them even shared the words state,university, and Iowa. Confusion ensues. What to do?
[![Image 3: Old Capital Image](https://www.foriowa.org/iowa-stories/images/0418OldGold1.png)](https://www.foriowa.org/iowa-stories/iowa-story.php?namer=true&isid=3#)General Catalogs Collection (RG 01.08)A view of the "Iowa State University" campus in Iowa City—not Ames—from the 1870-71 General Catalog.

**Mason Ladd**(23BA), dean of the State University of Iowa College of Law, anticipated this situation in 1957, when officials at Ames proposed renaming that campus. Ladd, in a Dec. 7, 1957, memo to SUI president **Virgil Hancher** (18BA, 24JD, 64LLD), pointed out that changing the Ames campus name to Iowa State University would be an “unconstitutional act. … Furthermore, it would involve great confusion in our statutes and require material revision in wording throughout the Code where either the State College or the University are mentioned.” (Papers of Mason Ladd, Box 6, folder “Brief – SUI Change of Name”) Apparently, President Hancher did not pursue Dean Ladd’s objection—or if he did was not successful—and ISC became ISU in 1959.
By 1964, the name confusion that Ladd predicted became reality, frustrating SUI officials. **Howard Bowen**(35PhD), by then president of the Iowa City campus, had an answer: Shorten the name of SUI in everyday usage to the University of Iowa, while retaining its full, original name for legal and other purposes. On Oct. 22, 1964, the Board of Regents approved a resolution authorizing just that (Board of Regents minutes, Oct. 21–24, 1964, pages 170–171).
To this day, people still occasionally (and understandably) confuse the names of Iowa’s public universities. Old Gold and his colleagues at Iowa Agricultural College and Model Farm/Iowa State College of Agricultural and Mechanic Arts/Iowa State University of Science and Technology and Iowa State Normal School/Iowa State Teachers College/State College of Iowa/University of Northern Iowa are always pleased to clear up this question.

For the University of Iowa, lots of history and a little confusion
![Image 1: The Pentacrest](https://www.foriowa.org/iowa-stories/images/0418OldGold3.png)Frederick W. Kent Collection of Photographs, UI Special Collections The University of Iowa’s Pentacrest in 1958.
**_Editor’s note: In Old Gold, University archivist David McCartney looks back at the UI’s history and tradition through materials housed in University Archives, Department of Special Collections, University of Iowa Libraries._**
If Old Gold had a list of top-10-asked reference questions at the University Archives (and well he should), surely one of them would be: When did the State University of Iowa become known simply as the University of Iowa?
Variations on that theme include: Weren’t we once also known as Iowa State University? Aren’t we still officially the State University of Iowa? Has confusion ensued?
